title: Quality and accuracy of clear aligner Arabic information on Instagram: A content-based analysis
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 264 Arabic-language Instagram posts about clear aligner therapy. Each post's claims were coded against evidence-based orthodontic guidelines and a health-misinformation framework into balanced facts / selected facts / non-facts / no claim. The 'non-facts' category (claims contradicting established evidence, exaggerating benefits, unsupported promises) is an explicit falsity/misleadingness judgement against an external ground truth, and is reported as a share of a stated denominator (94/264 = 35.61%). That is a CONTENT prevalence estimate, so the paper is eligible.

estimates.country: 13 countries (Arabic-language posts; 56% originating from Saudi Arabia)
estimates.date: Posts collected on 21 April 2025 (hashtag frequency assessment 14-20 April 2025)
estimates.measure_type: % of Arabic Instagram clear-aligner posts whose claims were coded as non-factual (contradicting evidence / exaggerated / unsupported promises)
estimates.value_raw: Non-facts 94 (35.61%) of 264 posts; text: 'mainly were non-factual (36%; Table 1)'
estimates.denominator: 264 Arabic-language Instagram posts about clear aligner therapy retained after screening (280 retrieved from 14 hashtags, 16 duplicates excluded)
estimates.definition: Post classified 'Non-facts': 'Posts making claims that contradict established evidence, exaggerate benefits or make unsupported promises inconsistent with systematic reviews and clinical guidelines.'
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Claim accuracy assessment was based on established health misinformation evaluation frameworks and evidence-based orthodontic treatment guidelines'; non-facts = 'statements inconsistent with peer-reviewed orthodontic literature'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two primary coders with orthodontic backgrounds and Arabic fluency (KA, SA) coded every post independently and blinded to each other; an orthodontic specialist (NA) arbitrated the 47 disagreements (17.8%); majority (2 of 3) rule. Reliability on a stratified random sample of 50 posts: claim accuracy categories Cohen's kappa = 0.87. Criteria drawn from Faerber & Kreling's false/misleading advertising framework and the Angle Society of Europe clear-aligner consensus.
estimates.moderator_quote: On 21 April 2025, posts were collected using a stratified random sampling approach to minimise selection bias and ensure representation across engagement levels. For each hashtag, posts were initially sorted chronologically (most recent 500 posts) to avoid Instagram's engagement-based algorithm bias. Posts were then stratified into three engagement tertiles ... yielding 20 posts per hashtag for a total target sample of 280 posts.
estimates.notes: Denominator is all posts in the sample (including the 52 'no claim' posts), so this is a share of items that exist in the sampled corpus -> CONTENT. denom_selection=curated because the frame is 14 pre-selected hashtags truncated to the most recent 500 posts each, then 20 sampled per hashtag; within that frame selection was stratified random. population_scope=professional because every post came from an orthodontist (42%), a dental interest group/clinic (54.2%) or a dentist (3.8%), not from lay users. breadth=misleading rather than false because the numerator mixes claims contradicting evidence with exaggerations and unsupported promises. Abstract rounds the same value to 36%; the verbatim table value 35.61 is used.  QUOTE NOTE: the v2 text extraction interleaves the article's columns, so no longer contiguous span of the published sentence is recoverable; source_quote is the exact contiguous span carrying the value, and the full published sentence is: "Most posts were in photo format (75%), posted by dental interest groups (58%), and were promotional (63%), with a marketing theme (48%), primarily for clear aligner product advertisements (61%) and mainly were non-factual (36%; Table 1)." (Results, p. 4); the quote used here is the Table 1 cell.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Balanced facts 45 (17.05%) and No claim 52 (19.7%) are the two remaining accuracy categories; neither is a misinformation numerator, so no row. (2) Table 3 breaks claim accuracy down by post format, poster role, post content, post theme and post type (e.g. non-facts 57.9% of marketing posts, 52.1% of self-promotion posts, 7.2% of educational posts). These are sub-group splits of the same 264 posts, not separate country/platform/measure cells, and the paper's headline is the overall 36%, so they are collapsed into the single main row per the one-row rule. (3) '99% of orthodontic patients use social media applications' is cited from another study (ref 32) and is not an eligible value (R8). (4) The 1,058,700-post initial pool is a hashtag volume estimate, not a screened denominator. (5) No exposure, sharing, recall or concentration measure is reported anywhere in the paper.

rob.design: Prospective cross-sectional content analysis. Frame: 14 Arabic clear-aligner hashtags chosen from 28 candidates by post volume, relevance and geographic diversity over 14-20 April 2025; on 21 April 2025 each hashtag's most recent 500 posts were stratified into engagement tertiles and 20 were drawn at random per hashtag (280 retrieved, 16 duplicates removed, 264 analysed). Sample size justified by G*Power (d=0.3, alpha=0.05, power 95%, 220 needed). Two independent trained coders, blinded to each other and to engagement metrics; senior orthodontist arbitrated the 47 disagreements (17.8%); 2-of-3 majority rule. Reliability on a stratified random 50-post subsample: inclusion decisions kappa=0.85; claim accuracy kappa=0.87; content categorisation kappa=0.79-0.84; poster role kappa=0.91; engagement ICC=0.98. Non-parametric tests with Bonferroni correction. Limitations acknowledged: single platform, fixed hashtag list, Saudi-dominant sample.
